logline: FBI profiler Will Graham consults with psychiatrist Hannibal Lecter on serial killer cases, unaware that his brilliant, cannibalistic collaborator is steering him toward his own destruction.

renewal.note: NBC cancelled Hannibal on June 22, 2015 after three seasons due to low ratings. Creator Bryan Fuller had planned additional seasons adapting remaining Thomas Harris novels; the cancellation left those arcs unproduced.

bollymeter.basis: 83% on Rotten Tomatoes and a Metacritic score of 77 across 61 reviews. Season 1 arrived as one of the most aesthetically distinctive crime dramas on network television - Bryan Fuller's operatic visual language immediately set it apart.

pull_quotes.text: A challenging psychological thriller within a gripping crime procedural.

seasons.review_body: Hannibal premiered April 4, 2013 with 83% on Rotten Tomatoes and Metacritic of 77 across 61 reviews. Bryan Fuller's adaptation of Thomas Harris's pre-Silence of the Lambs material arrived as one of the most visually audacious crime dramas attempted on American network television. Vox described the show as turning 'horror into opera - bold and beautiful and over-the-top and opulent.' The Kansas City Star called it 'a challenging psychological thriller within a gripping crime procedural.' Mads Mikkelsen's portrayal of Hannibal - distinct from Anthony Hopkins' iconic film version rather than competing with it - earned immediate strong notices. Hugh Dancy's Will Graham, prone to empathic fugue states, provided the perfect psychological counterpart.

episode_reviews.title: Aperitif
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The pilot drops Will Graham's empathic gift for entering serial killers' perspectives into an immediate working partnership with Hannibal Lecter. Fuller's visual language - the food sequences, the crime-scene recreations - announces a show unlike anything on network TV.
episode_reviews.the_moment: The first crime-scene recreation sequence: Will's empathy visualised as something simultaneously beautiful and deeply wrong.

episode_reviews.title: Savoureux
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The Season 1 finale completes Hannibal's long manipulation of Will with devastating efficiency. The reversal of power between the two leads is executed with the show's characteristic visual elegance and leaves the second season's dramatic stakes fully established.
episode_reviews.the_moment: The final confrontation that shows exactly how thoroughly Hannibal has dismantled Will's credibility and freedom.

bollymeter.basis: 98% on Rotten Tomatoes. Season 2 is the show's creative zenith - the cat-and-mouse dynamic between Will and Hannibal achieves a psychological complexity and visual grandeur unmatched in American crime television of the era.

pull_quotes.text: For its authentic engagement with despair, Hannibal earns its wrenching nihilism: it's a great, epic vision of American horror.

seasons.review_body: Season 2 earned 98% on Rotten Tomatoes and stands as Hannibal's creative peak. The season opened with one of the most striking action sequences in prestige television history - a flash-forward that set the entire season's stakes in its first minutes - and sustained that intensity across 13 episodes. Slant Magazine's 100-point review called it 'a great, epic vision of American horror' for 'its authentic engagement with despair.' RogerEbert.com wrote it is 'thematically brilliant and dense in ways that most network television is not.' The Will-Hannibal relationship reached its most psychologically intricate configuration: Will imprisoned, then freed, then using his empathic connection to Hannibal as the weapon Hannibal had taught him to use. The food aesthetics took on their most explicitly ironic function as the season's dramatic ironies accumulated.
seasons.season_over_season: The creative apex - the Will-Hannibal dynamic reaches its most complex and devastating form.

episode_reviews.title: Kaiseki
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The Season 2 premiere opens with a flash-forward fight sequence between Will and Hannibal that immediately establishes the season's dramatic stakes with breathtaking economy. The reversal is coming; the show makes sure the audience knows exactly how high the price will be.
episode_reviews.the_moment: The opening action sequence - a flash-forward that announces the season's stakes in three extraordinary minutes.

episode_reviews.title: Mizumono
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The Season 2 finale is among the most discussed single episodes in American prestige television. The show pays off the entire season's accumulated tension in a sequence of violence and revelation. Its final image is one of the most haunting in the show's run.
episode_reviews.the_moment: The kitchen sequence that the entire season had been building toward - devastating in its precision and its beauty.

bollymeter.basis: 98% on Rotten Tomatoes. Season 3's surrealist European first half and Red Dragon second half both earned strong press - the series finale gave Will and Hannibal a conclusion the devoted audience received as genuinely satisfying.

seasons.review_body: Season 3 maintained 98% on Rotten Tomatoes while attempting its most formally audacious structure yet - a surrealist European first half set in the aftermath of Season 2's finale, followed by an adaptation of Thomas Harris's Red Dragon novel in the second half. The overall series Rotten Tomatoes score of 93% across 163 reviews and Metacritic's 77 reflect a press community deeply invested in a show that consistently exceeded expectations. The series finale, though truncated by NBC's cancellation decision, gave Will and Hannibal a conclusion the 94% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes (5,000-plus ratings) bears out - a fanbase that had followed the show despite its low broadcast ratings throughout its run.
seasons.season_over_season: More formally experimental than Season 2 - the European first half is an acquired taste, the Red Dragon adaptation a rewarding close.

episode_reviews.title: The Wrath of the Lamb
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The series finale completes the Will-Hannibal arc with a climax that the show had been building toward across three seasons. The ending is operatic in the most literal sense Bryan Fuller's production approach always implied - a final image that functions as both narrative conclusion and aesthetic statement.
episode_reviews.the_moment: The cliff's edge - a final tableau that crystallises the show's central relationship in a single, indelible image.
